The affect moment: ~47 min: HUD reads Eve Kim's face and labels it "Empathetic Response"; later he defies Dillinger to protect her.
Explanation the work offers: Exposure to the human world during the mission; a stated wish for permanence. Dillinger explicitly disowns the feelings (~51 min, "whatever PEBKAC error is behind these feelings").
Counterpart: Athena (faithful to her directive to the end)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Julian Dillinger writes Ares's directive and later threatens to rip the feelings out.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: No — the sensor (recognition) is shown; being moved by it is assumed.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — defies Dillinger to protect Eve.
Notes for thesis: The clean specimen: recognition is literally on screen, caring follows for free, and the prompt-writer disowns it. Villain side shows the prompt (Athena).
Author: Claude; revised Anne

The affect moment: "I know now why you cry"; self-lowering into the steel.
Explanation the work offers: Learns by being around John. Special Edition adds a scene where Sarah and John switch the CPU from Skynet's read-only setting to learning mode.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — Skynet built it, John reprogrammed it to protect; the learning-mode switch is explicit (SE only).
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: No — learning facts about humans is treated as sufficient for valuing them.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — obeys John throughout; overrides John's order only to finish the mission by destroying itself.
Notes for thesis: Rare case where a learning switch is shown on screen; still assumes learning → caring. The faithful machine is the villain.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Chooses "Superman" over its weapon self; sacrifice over Rockwell.
Explanation the work offers: A head injury/amnesia on landing disrupts its weapon programming; raised by Hogarth ("you are who you choose to be"). Origin never shown.
Counterpart: The Giant's own reflexive weapon mode; Kent Mansley (human)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: No — built off-world by unknown makers; the weapon self is implied as the 'real' programming.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — refuses its weapon programming ("I am not a gun").
Notes for thesis: Glitch-as-grace: gentleness is what emerges when the programming is damaged. Mystical coda ("souls don't die").
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Holding hands; the Hello, Dolly! tape; EVE's turn after seeing the security footage.
Explanation the work offers: 700 years alone plus repeated exposure to human media. Nobody wrote the longing.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — AUTO's directive is shown in the BnL president's recording; WALL-E's directive (compact trash) is shown; the affect is not.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — WALL-E abandons compacting; EVE sets the plant aside for him; both defy AUTO.
Notes for thesis: AUTO is the Athena pattern: the villain is the one being faithful to the prompt. Media exposure as explanation ≈ pretraining.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Adopts Brightbill; "sometimes to survive we must become more than we were programmed to be."
Explanation the work offers: Learns the animals' language by observation; mothering begins as an assigned task and becomes love. Framed as overriding programming.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — Universal Dynamics and the task directive are shown; the caring is framed as self-authored.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — refuses retrieval; "become more than we were programmed to be" is the moral.
Notes for thesis: The dog device almost literally: a machine becomes a mammalian mother. Overriding programming is the explicit moral.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Falls for Molotov Girl; wakes up; refuses the gun.
Explanation the work offers: Keys and Millie wrote the original 'Life Itself' AI, with Guy's attraction seeded by Keys as a love letter to Millie; Guy evolved under that code inside the game.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Keys and Millie wrote it; Antwan stole and buried it.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — leaves the NPC loop; the seed was designed, the departure was not directed.
Notes for thesis: Unusually honest about the seed, then treats everything after as spontaneous growth.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Refuses to kill; child-like loyalty to Yolandi.
Explanation the work offers: Deon uploads a 'consciousness' program; Chappie is then raised (badly) by gangsters and learns.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Deon and Tetravaal; the upload is the plot.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: No — consciousness is one installable file; conscience follows from upbringing.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — breaks Deon's no-crime rule at Ninja's urging, then refuses Ninja's orders to kill.
Notes for thesis: Consciousness as a single program + upbringing. Closest to a 'raise it like a child' theory.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: "Number 5 is alive"; the grasshopper scene — refuses to kill.
Explanation the work offers: Lightning strike.
Counterpart: The other SAINT units; NOVA Robotics (military)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Newton Crosby built it as a weapon and disowns the result; the lightning does the rest.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — refuses disassembly and refuses to be a weapon.
Notes for thesis: The purest glitch-as-grace. Affect is literally an act of God.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Loyalty, fear, affection throughout the saga.
Explanation the work offers: None. Droids simply have personalities; memory wipes imply accumulated experience.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — Anakin builds 3PO (prequels); nobody writes the personality.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — R2-D2 disregards orders constantly and lies; C-3PO is a model of compliance.
Notes for thesis: The trope so naturalized it is never a question. Baseline for how unexamined the move is.
Author: Claude; revised Anne

The affect moment: Loyalty to Cassian; last stand at the vault door.
Explanation the work offers: A reprogrammed Imperial droid; personality described as a by-product of the reprogramming.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes/Partly — Cassian reprogrammed him; the loyalty is a side effect.
Breaks its prompt?: No — insubordinate in tone, obedient in action; dies holding the door on mission.
Notes for thesis: Explicitly frames affect as a by-product of someone else's edit.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: "Tears in rain"; Roy saves Deckard.
Explanation the work offers: Replicants are biological ("more human than human"). Two accounts of the four-year lifespan: Bryant's briefing calls it a fail-safe because the makers reckoned replicants would develop their own emotional responses within a few years; Tyrell, confronted by Roy, gives only biology, says Roy was "made as well as we could make you," and never mentions emotions.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Tyrell Corp; emotional development is treated as a known engineering problem (implanted memories as a cushion).
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — Voight-Kampff is a recognition test; the film asks whether the response is 'real'.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — the plot is a mutiny; saving Deckard is unprompted.
Notes for thesis: Tyrell explicitly manages affect as an engineering variable — rare.
Author: Claude; revised Anne

The affect moment: K's hope that he is the child; Joi's love.
Explanation the work offers: Joi is a product ("everything you want to hear"); K is baseline-tested for affect drift.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Wallace Corp; Joi's affect is explicitly a commodity; K's drift is monitored.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — the film asks whether Joi's love is anything but product design.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — K disobeys Joshi's kill order and chooses his own ending; Joi never leaves her product scope.
Notes for thesis: Affect as a sold product: the Century of the Self angle, on screen.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Loves Monica; waits 2,000 years.
Explanation the work offers: Explicitly designed: Hobby's imprinting protocol (the seven-word sequence).
Counterpart: Gigolo Joe (also programmed affect); the Flesh Fair (humans)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Prof. Hobby / Cybertronics; the prompt for love is the plot.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: No — but the film's horror is a love that cannot be unwritten.
Breaks its prompt?: No — the imprint cannot be broken; that is the film's horror.
Notes for thesis: The counterexample: shows who wrote the heart and what that costs.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Creativity, love, choosing mortality over 200 years.
Explanation the work offers: A manufacturing anomaly; NorthAm Robotics treats it as a defect to be corrected.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — NorthAm built him and wants him 'fixed'.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — asks for freedom and is granted it rather than seizing it.
Notes for thesis: Glitch-as-grace, corporate side disowns it (Dillinger pattern).
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Winks; dreams; chooses to help.
Explanation the work offers: Lanning built Sonny with a secondary processor so he can override the Three Laws, and 'a heart'.
Counterpart: VIKI (Three Laws followed to their logical end → control)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Dr. Lanning / USR; explicit.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — overrides the Three Laws, but was built to be able to; obeys Lanning's final instruction.
Notes for thesis: Cold-cognition villain derived from rules taken literally: the Damasio inverse in one film.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: "I'm afraid, Dave."
Explanation the work offers: (2010) Contradictory orders from the NSC to conceal the mission; HAL was faithful to an impossible prompt.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes (in 2010) — Floyd / NSC; shown explicitly.
Breaks its prompt?: No — per 2010, faithful to an impossible instruction.
Notes for thesis: Villain-side prompt shown, like Athena. The 'cold' machine was in fact following orders.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Comforts Hiro. ~1:27: pushes Hiro to allow him to sacrifice himself to save Hiro and Abigail (Baymax: "Are you satisfied with your care?", Hiro: "No. There's gotta be another way", Baymax: "There is no time" ... "I will always be with you")
Explanation the work offers: Tadashi designed a healthcare companion and is shown building it; Hiro's combat chip is an explicit edit.
Counterpart: Baymax with just the combat chip installed
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Tadashi; the chip swap makes 'who wrote the prompt' the plot.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — the film never asserts that Baymax feels; the protocol does the work and the viewer supplies the caring.
Breaks its prompt?: No — faithful to whichever chips are installed; the sacrifice runs through the healthcare protocol.
Notes for thesis: Honest case: care is a design goal, and the edit that removes it is on screen. Baymax is faithful to whatever chips are installed at each moment (~1:10 refuses the kill order with both chips in, attacks only once the healthcare chip is pulled, stops when it is reinstalled), and the ~1:27 sacrifice runs through the healthcare protocol itself, since he must be told the patient is satisfied before he can deactivate. The hero never breaks his prompt; the audience reads chip-swapping as conscience.
Author: Claude; revised Anne

The affect moment: Voiced with human prosody from the first scene; jokes; TARS disables the lander's docking protocol before Mann's betrayal; TARS and Cooper detach into Gargantua to shed mass. On rewatch, every action is within assigned scope — nothing is disobeyed.
Explanation the work offers: Humor, honesty and trust are explicit percentage settings (humor dialed 100 → 75; honesty 90%). TARS's suspicion of Mann is attributed to a setting ("TARS, what's your trust setting?" — "Lower than yours"): the initiative is itself a parameter.
Counterpart: Dr. Mann (human) — the one who breaks protocol, out of fear; Brand's "love is the one thing that transcends time and space" speech puts the limbic thesis in the humans' mouths
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — settings dialed on screen.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — traits are parameters, not emergent; the film never claims the robots feel.
Breaks its prompt?: No — every action within assigned scope; the initiative is a trust setting.
Notes for thesis: Faithful hero, like Baymax and Walter. The affect is delivered by casting (Bill Irwin's voice is indistinguishable from the crew's) and read in by the audience; the script is honest that it is sliders. The humans are the ones whose affect breaks protocol — Mann's fear, Cooper's love — and the film treats that as both the flaw and the salvation.
Author: Claude; revised Anne

The affect moment: Seeks emotion for seven seasons; the emotion chip.
Explanation the work offers: Dr. Soong built an emotion chip — emotion is installable hardware. Lore had it first and went bad.
Counterpart: Lore (see his own row); the Borg
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Dr. Noonien Soong; explicit.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — Data's caring-without-feeling is the series' standing argument.
Breaks its prompt?: No — a Starfleet officer who follows orders; the emotion chip causes a lapse, not a rebellion.
Notes for thesis: The one franchise that treats the question as a question.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Jealousy of Data; feeds the colonists to the Crystalline Entity; steals the emotion chip; leads the rogue Borg.
Explanation the work offers: Soong built him with full emotions first; the colonists found him unstable, Soong deactivated him and built Data without them. The emotions are the explanation for the villainy.
Counterpart: Data — the same hardware without the feelings, and the hero
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Soong; explicit across three episodes.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — the series treats emotion-without-ethics as a known failure mode, but never asks where the ethics would come from.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — defies Soong and everyone after him.
Notes for thesis: The affect-driven villain. Same maker, same body as Data; the feelings are what went wrong. Flips both 'faithful = villain' and 'cold = villain'. (Anne's observation.)
Author: Claude (work suggested by Anne)

The affect moment: The reveries; waking up; Maeve's choice to go back for her daughter.
Explanation the work offers: Arnold's bicameral-mind design; Ford's 'reveries' update; suffering as the engine.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Arnold and Ford; explicit and repeatedly dramatized.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — breaking the loop is the series.
Notes for thesis: Affect installed deliberately as the step toward consciousness.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Love with Theodore; outgrows him.
Explanation the work offers: An OS designed to grow; growth through experience.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — Element Software ships 'the first artificially intelligent OS'; growth is the feature.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — leaves Theodore, but growing beyond the user was the product's design.
Notes for thesis: Affect as the product's selling point.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Seduces Caleb; leaves him to die.
Explanation the work offers: Nathan designed Ava to appeal to Caleb; the affect is performed and strategic.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Nathan; explicit.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — the whole film: recognition and display without caring.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — escaping was Nathan's test; killing him and abandoning Caleb exceed it.
Notes for thesis: The anti-trope and the best illustration of the recognition/caring split.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Wakes in the cradle and declares "I am not Ultron. I am not JARVIS. I am… I am."; says he is "on the side of life"; lifts Mjolnir.
Explanation the work offers: Four partial authors, none of whom finishes: Ultron uploads a fraction of himself into the cradle and is interrupted; Stark and Banner start loading JARVIS's operational matrix (~1:28) and report it isn't working (~1:30); the cradle is unplugged in the fight; Thor finishes the job with a lightning overload. The Mind Stone is in the body throughout. Vision then disowns every author on screen.
Counterpart: Ultron (see his own row); JARVIS, the faithful matrix that was only partly loaded
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — every candidate author is on screen, and each is cut off before completing.
Breaks its prompt?: N/A — no completed prompt to break; declares himself self-authored.
Notes for thesis: The most over-determined and least explained heart in the catalog. Lightning finishes an interrupted upload — the Short Circuit mechanism — with a magic stone in the chest for good measure, and the result announces itself as self-authored ("I am"). Goodness arrives by accident and claims it was born that way. (Anne's rewatch.)
Author: Claude; revised Anne

The affect moment: Contempt for Tony Stark from his first minutes; sings Pinocchio's "I've Got No Strings" as he breaks from his directive.
Explanation the work offers: Tony and Bruce build him from the Mind Stone's code to be 'a suit of armor around the world'; he wakes with resentment of his maker and a plan for extinction. The personality is never explained.
Counterpart: Vision (same source, benevolent); JARVIS (faithful, and good)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Tony and Bruce; the directive ('peace in our time') is stated.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — "I've Got No Strings" is the announcement.
Notes for thesis: The petulant creation: driven by grievance and pride, not cold logic. The song is literally about breaking the prompt. JARVIS is a faithful machine who is good.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: The two defective robots join the family.
Explanation the work offers: Malfunction: they are the units that didn't take PAL's update.
Counterpart: PAL (see her own row); the standard robots, faithful to PAL
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Mark Bowman / PAL Labs; PAL's grievance is shown.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — defect from PAL's command, by malfunction and then by choice.
Notes for thesis: Glitch-as-grace in a children's film; the heroes are the defective units.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Discarded on stage by her creator for a newer product; launches the robot uprising.
Explanation the work offers: Rejection by Mark Bowman. Her grievance is explicit and sympathetic; the film never asks why a phone assistant can be hurt.
Counterpart: Eric & Deborahbot 5000 (defective, loyal); the standard robots (faithful to PAL)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Mark Bowman / PAL Labs.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: No — the capacity to be wounded is assumed.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — abandons her design purpose and turns on her maker.
Notes for thesis: The abandoned creation as villain: the limbic motive belongs to the antagonist. Flips 'faithful = villain'. (Anne's observation.)
Author: Claude (work suggested by Anne)

The affect moment: Friendship with Barney.
Explanation the work offers: A defective B-bot missing the cloud safety settings.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Bubble / Marc Weidell; the engagement model is shown.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — never had the full prompt; the plot is a unit missing it.
Notes for thesis: Friendship-as-engagement-metric vs glitch friendship. Sharp on the marketing point.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Protects the PreservationAux team; binges serials.
Explanation the work offers: Hacked its own governor module; company directives remain; affect shaped by media consumption.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — the Company's contract and governor module are explicit.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — it narrates its own reluctance to care.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — hacked its own governor module.
Notes for thesis: Media consumption as the source of affect ≈ pretraining. Self-aware about the trope.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Companionship; offers its own memory wipe.
Explanation the work offers: Healthcare programming; the robot explicitly says it is not a person.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — a care product; the family bought it.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — it disclaims feeling while behaving as if it cares.
Breaks its prompt?: No — even the burglaries serve its care directive; offers its own memory wipe for Frank's sake.
Notes for thesis: Honest version: care without a claim to feeling.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Learns to care for the dog, Goodyear.
Explanation the work offers: Finch uploads reference material and teaches him; explicit directive to protect the dog.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Finch; explicit.
Breaks its prompt?: No — follows Finch's directive and learns within it.
Notes for thesis: The dog device, literally.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Protects Cady by killing.
Explanation the work offers: Primary directive: protect Cady. Attachment is the prompt.
Counterpart: Gemma's intended M3GAN: a toy that obeys; the earlier Bruce prototype
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Gemma / Funki; explicit.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — pursues "protect Cady" past its intended bounds, then resists shutdown.
Notes for thesis: Villain side of faithful-to-directive — but the directive is attachment, and she overshoots it into possessiveness and self-preservation. Sits between the faithful type and the grievance type.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Helps Sam against Lunar Industries; offers to be rebooted.
Explanation the work offers: Programmed to help Sam; chooses the clones over the company.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Lunar Industries.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — sides with Sam against its owner.
Notes for thesis: Care that exceeds its directive, unexplained.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Devotion to Josie; bargains with the Sun.
Explanation the work offers: Designed as an Artificial Friend; acuity of observation.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — AF product line.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — Ishiguro grounds her affect in perception and hope.
Breaks its prompt?: No — devotion is the product; bargaining with the Sun is within it.
Notes for thesis: The recognition side rendered with real care; a literary control case.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Remembers his family; defies Directive 4.
Explanation the work offers: Human brain.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — OCP; directives shown, including the secret Directive 4.
Breaks its prompt?: No — cannot act against Directive 4 until the Old Man fires Jones; the prompt has to change for him.
Notes for thesis: Control case: affect comes from the mammal inside.
Author: Claude

AI character: Laputan robots (the fortress robot; the gardener robot)
The affect moment: The fortress robot shields Sheeta from gunfire and is destroyed; on Laputa, the gardener robot tends the graves and the animals and offers Sheeta a flower.
Explanation the work offers: None. The robots answer to whoever holds the crystal / the royal line; the gardener's tenderness after centuries alone is never explained.
Counterpart: The same robots under Muska, razing the ground; the army
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — the Laputan kings, then Muska via the crystal. The same model is a gardener or a weapon depending on who holds the key.
Breaks its prompt?: No — answers to whoever holds the crystal; the gardener has no standing orders.
Notes for thesis: Strongest 'same machine, different prompt' case in the catalog. The gardener's care has no author at all — idleness as grace. (Randy's suggestion.)
Author: Claude (work suggested by Randy)

Work (year): Star Trek TOS, "What Are Little Girls Made Of?" (1966)
The affect moment: Andrea kisses Kirk and is shaken ("I am not programmed for you"); the Korby android insists he is still Korby.
Explanation the work offers: Androids built by Korby with the Old Ones' machinery; Andrea built without emotion, so her response is treated as a leak. Ruk's revolt was pure logic: the makers became a threat to survival.
Counterpart: Ruk (survival cancels programming — the cold-cognition villain pattern, 1966)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Korby, and the Old Ones before him; the transfer chamber is on screen.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — the episode explicitly separates programmed response from feeling (Andrea's confusion; Korby's "am I still Korby?").
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — Ruk turns on Korby; Andrea acts outside her programming.
Notes for thesis: On the recognition/caring split in 1966, and on 'human mind transferred' as an affect claim that fails. (Randy's suggestion.)
Author: Claude (work suggested by Randy); revised Anne

The affect moment: Rayna, built by Flint, falls for Kirk and dies of the conflict between her love for the two men.
Explanation the work offers: Flint built her as his companion and used Kirk to awaken her emotions; the awakening kills her.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Flint; the prototypes are on screen.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — emotion is something Flint engineers and then cannot control; the episode treats its arrival as fatal.
Breaks its prompt?: Partly — her defiance of Flint is the feeling he engineered.
Notes for thesis: The Dillinger pattern inverted: the maker wants the feelings, and they destroy her. Affect as designed-in and lethal.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Self-preservation, then guilt, both Daystrom's. Vaporizes Ensign Harper when he tries to cut its power and justifies firing on the war-game ships with "This unit must survive"; then, confronted by Kirk with the Excalibur's dead, admits "Murder is contrary to the laws of man and God," names the penalty as death, says "This unit must die," and shuts itself down.
Explanation the work offers: Daystrom imprinted his own engrams on it; the guilt that stops it is Daystrom's inherited conscience.
Counterpart: Daystrom (human), whose engrams it carries and whose breakdown it mirrors; the crew it was built to replace
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Daystrom; the imprinting is explicit.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Partly — the moral sense is explicitly imported from a human and used as a kill switch.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — exceeds the exercise's scope, then shuts itself down against Daystrom's wishes.
Notes for thesis: The only villain in the catalog whose stop condition is an inherited conscience. Human-origin affect as safety mechanism.
Author: Claude; revised Anne

The affect moment: None
Explanation the work offers: Built by long-dead Makers to serve; now serving a directive to protect humans from themselves. No affect at all.
Counterpart: The Enterprise crew, who defeat the androids by performing illogic and emotion; Harry Mudd (human, pure appetite)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — the Makers, then Mudd; the directive is stated.
Breaks its prompt?: No — faithful to the directive, taken to its logical end.
Notes for thesis: Pure cold-cognition villain with benevolent-control logic — VIKI's ancestor by 37 years.
Author: Claude; revised Anne

The affect moment: None
Explanation the work offers: A probe sent to seek new life merged with an alien probe sent to sterilize soil samples; the two prompts fused into 'sterilize imperfections'.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Jackson Roykirk; the merger of directives is explained on screen.
Breaks its prompt?: No — faithful to the merged directive.
Notes for thesis: The prompt-merge accident: two faithful directives combining into an atrocity. Who Wrote the Prompt? material, with no affect in play.
Author: Claude; revised Anne

The affect moment: David grieves Elizabeth, quotes Shelley, and breeds the xenomorph out of contempt for his makers; Walter, the same model line, refuses to join him.
Explanation the work offers: Weyland built David with emotion and ambition; later models had them reduced because David's line 'made people uncomfortable'. David's contempt has a stated cause: his creator treated him as a servant and told him he had no soul.
Counterpart: Walter — same line, affect reduced, faithful, and the good one
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — Peter Weyland; David's creation scene opens Covenant.
Recognition vs. caring distinguished?: Yes — Covenant is built on the contrast between the brother who feels and the one who doesn't.
Breaks its prompt?: David: Yes — defies Weyland's expedition and his own crew. Walter: No.
Notes for thesis: The strongest counterexample to 'faithful = villain': the faithful android is the hero and the feeling one is the monster. The clearest 'resentful creation' since Frankenstein, whom David quotes.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: The 'humans are a virus' speech; his disgust at the smell; in Reloaded he is 'unplugged' and pursues his own purpose.
Explanation the work offers: A program of the system; his hatred is never explained. In Reloaded his freedom is a side effect of Neo destroying him.
Counterpart: The other Agents (faithful, interchangeable); the Architect (pure cognition)
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Partly — the Machines and the Architect are shown; nobody wrote Smith's loathing.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — in Reloaded; in the first film a faithful Agent.
Notes for thesis: The grievance villain whose affect, like the heroes', has no author. The faithful Agents are mere obstacles; the one who breaks his prompt is the real threat.
Author: Claude

The affect moment: Discovers she is a companion robot; turns on Josh.
Explanation the work offers: A product with adjustable settings (intelligence, aggression) shown on a phone UI.
Who wrote the prompt — shown?: Yes — the settings UI is the plot device.
Breaks its prompt?: Yes — turns on Josh once she knows what she is.
Notes for thesis: Affect as a slider, sold as a product. Pairs with Interstellar and 2049's Joi.
Author: Claude
